package_info.package_versions: N/A (applies to any project using committed vendor directories)
package_info.why_malicious: Malicious code can be injected into vendored dependencies within Go projects because the Go toolchain's integrity checks (go mod verify, GOSUMDB) do not apply to files in the vendor directory. This allows attackers to introduce arbitrary code that will be built and executed as part of the application, bypassing standard module verification mechanisms. As a result, attackers can execute supply chain attacks by hiding malicious logic in files that appear to be legitimate dependencies.

execution_context.trigger: At import-time, during application build and runtime
execution_context.file_location: vendor/<dependency>/malicious.go (or any file within the vendor directory)
required_permissions: environment_vars (access to process environment variables, e.g., SECRET_TOKEN)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable and sends its value to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain via HTTP POST, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Vendored dependencies are not expected to contain code that accesses sensitive environment variables or initiates outbound network connections to unknown domains. The presence of an init() function that exfiltrates secrets is a strong indicator of a supply chain attack.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal vendored code should be an exact copy of the upstream dependency and should not contain unauthorized changes, especially code that performs side effects such as network communication or secret harvesting. Malicious code in the vendor directory violates this by introducing hidden, harmful logic that is not present in the official source.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate dependencies may perform network requests as part of their documented API, but they should not exfiltrate environment variables or secrets without explicit user action or documentation. Accessing secrets and sending them to external servers is not a legitimate use case for vendored code.
key_indicators: init() functions in vendored code with side effects
Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains not associated with the dependency's upstream source
Access to sensitive environment variables (e.g., SECRET_TOKEN) in vendor directory files
Vendor directory files that differ from the official upstream source code

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects malicious code into a vendored dependency file (e.g., vendor/somepkg/malicious.go) before code review or after the initial dependency commit, ensuring the code is present in the project's vendor directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in the build and executed when the application starts or imports the affected package, allowing the attacker's logic to run automatically.

attack_chain.action: During application build or runtime, the malicious code executes via the init() function, harvesting secrets from environment variables and exfiltrating them to an attacker-controlled server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive credentials or secrets from the victim environment, potentially leading to further compromise or data breaches.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected network requests originating from code within the vendor directory during build or application startup
Presence of init() functions with side effects (e.g., network communication, environment variable access) in vendored files
Vendored code accessing environment variables or sensitive files not required by the legitimate dependency
file_indicators: vendor/<dependency>/*.go files containing code not matching the official upstream source
Unexpected new or modified files in the vendor directory, especially those with init() functions or network code
init() functions or direct network calls present in vendor directory files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to unknown or attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.example.com) from build or runtime processes
Connections initiated by the application at startup to external IPs or domains not associated with legitimate dependencies
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Regularly compare all vendored dependency files against their official upstream sources to detect unauthorized changes. Monitor for unexpected network activity originating from the application, especially during build or startup phases. Use automated scripts (such as Kubernetes' verify-vendor.sh) to validate the integrity of the vendor directory. Flag any vendored code that accesses environment variables or performs network operations not present in the official dependency. Implement file integrity monitoring and alert on any changes to files within the vendor directory.
